source: Accretion Power
Matter falling onto a compact object releases about GMṁ/R, far more per kilogram than fusion near a neutron star.
Students think fusion always releases more energy per kilogram than falling.

When gas falls onto a compact object, it speeds up enormously, and when it is stopped or swirls into a disk, that energy turns into heat and light. In X-ray binaries a neutron star or a black hole pulls gas off a companion star; around supermassive black holes, accretion powers quasars. How much energy can falling release?

A kilogram falling from far away to the surface of a body of mass $M$ and radius $R$ loses potential energy $GM/R$ (with $U = 0$ at infinity). If that energy is radiated, a stream of $\dot m$ kilograms per second gives $$L_{\text{acc}} = \frac{GM\dot m}{R}.$$ Compare with rest energy: falling releases a fraction $GM/(Rc^2)$ of $mc^2$. For fusion of hydrogen into helium the fraction is 0.007. For a neutron star it is about 0.15 to 0.2.

Accretion releases $GM/R$ per kilogram, a fraction $\eta \approx GM/(Rc^2)$ of the rest energy. The more compact the object, the larger $\eta$: about $10^{-4}$ for a white dwarf, about 0.15 to 0.2 for a neutron star, and about 0.06 to 0.4 for gas spiraling into a black hole (depending on its spin), compared with 0.007 for hydrogen fusion.
Energy released by a kilogram of matter in different ways.

Thinking fusion always releases more energy per kilogram than falling. Fusion beats falling onto ordinary stars and white dwarfs, but near a neutron star or black hole, gravity wins by a wide margin: a kilogram dropped onto a neutron star releases more energy than fusing it would, about 25 times more. That is why the brightest steady X-ray sources in the sky, such as Scorpius X-1, are accreting neutron stars and black holes. Check: compare $GM/(Rc^2)$ with 0.007.
